findings.location: orientation[4].text, the fourth listed condition of the first further paragraph of s. 18(d1/2); repeated at worked_examples[3].steps[4]
findings.problem: The section compresses clause (4) of the first further paragraph of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d1/2) into "the pharmacist determines that it is authentic, valid, legitimate and legal in the state it came from and verifies it, and any delivery complies in full with that state's laws and regulations on the issuance and filling of prescriptions". Dropping the statute's words "to residents of another state" leaves "that state" pointing at its nearest antecedent, "the state it came from" (the originating state), whereas the statute attaches that full-compliance duty to the state of the residents to whom the controlled substances are delivered. worked_examples[3].steps[4] repeats the compression ("comply in full with that state's laws and regulations on the issuance and filling of prescriptions, and meet its reporting requirements").
findings.rationale: The statute reads: "any delivery of controlled substances to residents of another state shall be in full compliance with all laws and regulations of that state relative to the issuance and filling of prescriptions". "That state" is the residents' state, that is, the delivery state, which clause (6) confirms is "the state of residence of the person for whom the prescription was written". Clause (2) expressly contemplates an originating state that is only contiguous to the delivery state, so the two can differ and the attribution matters. The section states the rule correctly in five other places (comparison_tables[1].rows[0].cells[4], ma_vs_federal[2].text, decision_logic[6].action, retrieval_prompts[4].answer and worked_examples[3].resolution all say "the delivery state"), so this is an internal inconsistency in the orientation prose rather than a wrong rule taught throughout. Severity is Low: it can only change an answer on the narrow facts where the prescriber's state and the patient's state of residence differ, and the correct statement is available four more times in the same section. The repair is a four-word restoration of the statutory qualifier.

results.summary: Checked line by line against the current text of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18 and the two regulations the section cites. The three pathways and their reaches (schedules III to VI; nonnarcotic schedule II; narcotic schedule II limited to Maine or a contiguous state, "except as provided in section 18A"), the issuing conditions in each subsection's own words, the 30-day and five-day filling windows, the fill-not-presentation reading, the authenticity duty on all three pathways with telephone verification conditioned on schedules III to V in s. 18(c) and stated independently in (d) and (d1/2), the refusal protection on documented good faith efforts, the seven-day oral schedule III-V follow-up record, the anonymised 30-day Department copy measured from the filling and excluded from public-record status, the separate s. 18(d3/4) five-day initial-partial-dispensing limit with its 30-day same-pharmacy remainder and patient-record notation, the 105 CMR 721.055(A) presentation deadline triggered by the prescriber's out-of-state address on the prescription, 721.055(C), and the 247 CMR 9.04(10) day-one convention all check out exactly. Both further paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2) are reported accurately, including the six conditions, the long-term-care courier limb (which indeed states no prescriber condition of its own), and the point that neither makes the pharmacy a mail order pharmacy. All four listed practice questions (MA-Q-0027, MA-Q-0034, MA-Q-0124, MA-Q-0424) are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it. One Low defect: the orientation's compression of clause (4) of the first further paragraph attaches the full-compliance duty to the originating state rather than to the delivery state, contradicting the section's own comparison table, decision logic, retrieval prompt and worked-example resolution. MINOR_EDIT on that single clause.

results.summary: Nothing wrong found; the section is publishable as it stands. Every proposition was checked against current official text. Confirmed: the s. 1 controlled-substance definition and s. 2(a)'s sixth schedule make a Schedule VI drug a Massachusetts controlled substance; 105 CMR 700.002(A) to (E) adopt 21 CFR 1308.11 to 1308.15 and 700.002(F) leaves Schedule VI the residual prescription drugs; s. 23(f) conditions any refill on the original prescription; s. 17(c) and s. 23(g) impose the electronic mandate, s. 17(c) naming Schedule VI, and s. 23(h) clauses (i) to (vi) do not cover Schedule VI, so 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9) rests on residual clause (vii) with its 90-day written justification to the named committees, exactly as the section explains; 721.020(D)(3) (quantity of dosage units), (D)(4) (the veterinary, naloxone or opioid-antagonist, 721.070(A)(7) and (A)(12) blanks), (D)(6), (E) and (F) (signature plus facsimile or tamper-resistant form) and 721.040(A) (non-conforming format invalid and not to be filled) all survive the format exception; s. 20(a) keeps the immediate reduction to writing while s. 20(c) states in its own terms that its requirements do not apply to Schedule VI, and 721.070(B) is written for schedules II through V; 721.070(C) imposes no exception-verification duty on the receiving pharmacist; 721.010 defines a Failover as originating in a Schedule VI electronic prescription and 721.020(G)(1) to (3) states the three regulatory conditions, the third being that it not be for an Additional Drug. The Department's manual was read directly: it lists four conditions, the fourth being that the Failover must not be for an Additional Drug (giving gabapentin as the example), and it states verbatim the consequence the section teaches for a gabapentin Failover, with no follow-up owed by a qualifying Failover; the section's reference to "the fourth of the conditions" is accurate to the manual it cites there, and its reference to "the three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G)" is accurate to the regulation. 247 CMR 9.04(12) (one-year validity, no refill after one year, and the 14-day professional-judgment continuation conditioned on inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization, which governs the expiry branch as well as the no-refills branch), 9.04(10), 9.04(14)(b) (customer identifier expressly extended to a controlled substance classified as an additional drug), 9.04(15) (the institutional sterile compounding exclusion, which does list (10), (12) and (14)), 9.14(1) to (3) and 9.14(4)(a) to (c), and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) (certified technician transfers, Schedule VI only, with pharmacist-on-duty approval) are all reported exactly. 105 CMR 700.001, 700.012(A)(1), (A)(3), (A)(5) and (C)(8) were confirmed in the current text (PDF created 2024-02-02 and linked from the mass.gov regulation page dated 02/02/2024), including the additional-drug determination at (C)(8) and the customer-identifier duty reaching an additional drug; an obsolete 2017 copy of 105 CMR 700.000 is still downloadable from another mass.gov URL and numbers that determination (C)(7) and limits (A)(1) to a pharmacy in a health facility, but the section follows the current text and is right to do so. The section's reconciliation of the s. 24A(c) at-least-every-24-hours statutory limit with the 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) end-of-next-business-day regulatory limit is sound, correctly identifies the statute as the operative limit across a weekend, and is exactly the kind of two-source reconciliation that is usually missed. 21 CFR 1306.25(a) confirms the federal one-time transfer limit reaches only schedules III, IV and V. MA-Q-0116, MA-Q-0118 and MA-Q-0120 are each answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it.

findings.location: comparison_tables[0] ("Where each schedule is actually written down"), rows[6] ("Temporary Massachusetts placement"), cells[1], the "Federal provision" cell
findings.problem: The cell asserts "No counterpart in Part 1308" for temporary placement, in a table whose immediately preceding row uses the same formula to make the accurate point that Part 1308 stops at Schedule V. Part 1308 does contain a temporary-placement provision: 21 CFR 1308.11(h) is headed "Temporary listing of substances subject to emergency scheduling" and is where substances placed in Schedule I under 21 U.S.C. 811(h) are listed, which is the very federal route the same cell then describes M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2A(f) as invoking.
findings.rationale: The section's first learning objective is to separate federal controlled-substance status from Massachusetts scheduling consequences, so what Part 1308 does and does not contain is squarely within its declared scope, and this cell is the section's only statement about federal temporary scheduling. Read against the parallel Schedule VI row, "No counterpart in Part 1308" says Part 1308 has no temporary-placement provision, which is not so. Severity is Low: no Massachusetts dispensing, refill, transfer, partial-fill, record or reporting consequence turns on it, and the same cell directs the reader to 21 U.S.C. 811(h), so a candidate is not left believing federal law has no emergency-scheduling power. The repair is confined to that one cell.

results.summary: The federal and Massachusetts classification architecture is stated accurately and, in the places that usually go wrong, unusually precisely. Confirmed: the identical opening sentence of each of 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 and the Controlled Substances Code Number sentence in most of them; the 1308.12(b) and (b)(1) chapeaus, with the substance the table pinpoints at 1308.12(b)(1)(i) sitting exactly there, and every substance the worked example names present in that paragraph's exclusion list; 1308.13(e)(1)(ii), the 1308.15(c) chapeau with (c)(1), and the 1308.14(b)(1) beside 1308.15(c)(6) pair, all stated correctly with their quantity and formulation conditions. The worked example's resolution of the Schedule III / Schedule V overlap is textually right for a reason that is easy to get wrong and that the section identifies: 1308.13(e) carries the "unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule" preface and 1308.15(c) does not, so the narrower placement takes the preparation. 21 CFR 1300.01(a) and 21 U.S.C. 802(18) are quoted accurately, and the section is careful to say that an exclusion from 1308.12(b)(1) settles only that paragraph, noting that 1308.12(c) carries exceptions of its own. On the Massachusetts side, s. 2(a), s. 2(a1/2) (including the 30-day duty to mirror a new federal control), s. 2A (findings, 14-day notice period, up to one year, and the s. 2A(f) referral to the United States Attorney General under 21 U.S.C. 811(h)), s. 1, s. 23(f), s. 24A(a)(1) and (b), 105 CMR 700.001, 700.002(A) to (F) and 700.012(A)(1), (A)(2) and (C)(8) all match the current official text, including the additional-drug determination at (C)(8) in the current (2024) version of 105 CMR 700.000; an obsolete 2017 copy still downloadable from another mass.gov URL numbers it (C)(7), but the section follows the current text. The section lists no practice questions, so none can be contradicted. One Low defect, confined to a single table cell: "No counterpart in Part 1308" for temporary placement overlooks 21 CFR 1308.11(h). MINOR_EDIT.
